title: Oesophageal Atresia
subject: Surgery
summary: A congenital interruption of the oesophagus, usually with a tracheo‑oesophageal fistula, presenting in the newborn with drooling, choking and inability to swallow. Early recognition and surgical repair are life‑saving.

sections.p: Oesophageal atresia (OA) is a failure of the oesophagus to form a continuous tube. Most cases (≈85–90%) are type C: proximal blind pouch with a distal tracheo‑oesophageal fistula (TOF).

t.b: Look for drooling, choking, cyanosis on feeding – indicates aspiration risk
Shows a dilated proximal oesophageal pouch and a gasless abdomen if no distal fistula; a double‑bubble sign suggests OA without TOF

sections.p: Classification is based on fistula type (A–E). Type C is most common and carries the highest mortality if untreated. Severity is judged by associated anomalies and respiratory compromise.
b: Type C: proximal pouch + distal TOF
Type D: proximal pouch + proximal TOF
Type E: proximal pouch + distal TOF + proximal TOF

sections.p: Exact etiology unknown; multifactorial with genetic and environmental contributors. In low‑resource settings, maternal infections (e.g., rubella), malnutrition, and teratogenic drugs increase risk.

t.b: Detects polyhydramnios and fetal swallowing absence – early clue to OA

sections.p: Newborns present with excessive drooling, choking on feeds, cyanosis, and respiratory distress. Failure to pass a nasogastric tube beyond 10–15 cm is a key bedside sign.

t.b: If it stops at 10–15 cm, suspect OA; if it passes into stomach, rule out OA

sections.p: Investigations are limited in low‑resource settings; focus on clinical exam and plain radiography.

t.b: Shows air in proximal pouch and absence of gas in abdomen if no distal fistula; double‑bubble sign in OA without TOF
Can identify polyhydramnios and rule out other abdominal anomalies
Assess for hypoxia and hypercapnia due to aspiration

sections.p: Immediate complications include aspiration pneumonia, severe hypoxia, and cardiac failure. Delayed repair leads to malnutrition, failure to thrive, and chronic lung disease.

t.b: SpO2 <90% on room air indicates severe respiratory compromise

sections.p: Urgent stabilization, airway protection, and surgical repair within 24–48 h. Pre‑operative care includes suctioning, antibiotics for aspiration, and fluid resuscitation.

t.b: Primary anastomosis of oesophagus; if gap >5 cm, staged repair with esophagostomy and delayed reconstruction
Monitor for leak, infection, and feeding tolerance

sections.p: Post‑operative follow‑up focuses on growth, feeding, and monitoring for reflux or strictures. Prevention is limited but includes maternal health optimisation and avoidance of teratogens.

t.b: Detects strictures or leaks at 4–6 weeks post‑op

sections.p: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDA) and tracheoesophageal fistula without atresia can mimic respiratory distress but differ in feeding tolerance and imaging findings.
b: TEF without OA – feeds tolerated but coughing

sections.p: A normal chest X‑ray may miss a small distal fistula; polyhydramnios can be caused by other fetal swallowing disorders.
b: Small distal fistula may not show gasless abdomen

whenToSeekHelp: Severe cyanosis, apnea, or inability to pass a nasogastric tube beyond 10–15 cm in a newborn

faq.q: What is the most common type of oesophageal atresia?
faq.a: Type C – proximal blind pouch with a distal tracheo‑oesophageal fistula.

faq.q: Why is suctioning important before surgery?
faq.a: It removes pooled saliva and reduces aspiration risk during anesthesia.
Yes, polyhydramnios and absent fetal swallowing on ultrasound are early clues.

exam: A 2‑hour old infant presents with drooling and cyanosis on feeding. What is the first bedside test you perform? — Insert a nasogastric tube; if it stops at 10–15 cm, OA is likely.
During surgery you find a gap >5 cm between oesophageal ends. What is the next step? — Perform a staged repair with oesophagostomy and delayed reconstruction.

An infant with suspected OA is given ampicillin and gentamicin pre‑operatively. Why are these antibiotics chosen? — They cover common skin flora and enteric organisms that may cause aspiration pneumonia.
A chest X‑ray shows a double‑bubble sign. What does this indicate? — Oesophageal atresia without a distal fistula.
A newborn with OA develops severe hypoxia despite suctioning. What complication is most likely? — Aspiration pneumonia.
Post‑operative feeding is delayed. What investigation can identify a stricture? — Barium swallow at 4–6 weeks.
